did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 19 opens with a command to lament over the “princes of Israel”—that is, the nation’s leaders—rather than with a straightforward historical account alone.
Did you know? If Judah is compared to a lioness, she is portrayed as part of a world of lions: she lies down “among lions” and raises her cubs “among young lions.”
Did you know? The first cub is described as having learned to devour prey and even “devoured people”—an image of a leader whose harm to people and the land became a defining mark of his actions.
Did you know? The first cub was captured by a ruse and brought “with hooks” to the land of Egypt, emphasizing the prophet’s portrayal of the loss of his power and his exile.
Did you know? After the lioness realizes that her hope for the first cub is lost, she takes another cub and raises it as a young lion; this begins another portrayal of failed leadership.
Did you know? The second cub is not captured by a single nation alone: surrounding peoples and countries spread a net for him, and he is caught in their pit.

Did you know? After being captured, the second cub is brought to the king of Babylon so that his voice will no longer be heard on the mountains of Israel—a picture of his rule being brought to an end.
Did you know? In the second half of the lament, the image changes: instead of a lioness and her cubs, a fruitful vine appears, planted by abundant waters and bearing many branches.
Did you know? The vine’s branches are not merely signs of growth: they are called “strong rods” and are associated with rulers’ scepters, so the vine also symbolizes ruling power.

Did you know? The vine is uprooted, dries up in the east wind, and is consumed by fire; in the end, it has no “strong rod”—that is, no powerful branch fit to rule—and the lament concludes with the words, “It is a lament, and it has become a lament.”
